newsitem.title: UK: UK's Clarke rules out "radical" tax changes.
newsitem.headline: UK's Clarke rules out "radical" tax changes.

text.p: Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer, Kenneth Clarke, on Friday ruled out scrapping the nation's two-pronged direct tax structure in favour of a simplified single levy.

Clarke, attending the Conservative women's annual gathering of party faithful on Friday, was challenged by a conference delegate to scrap one of the two prongs - the national insurance tax - and introduce a simple, single tax charge.
But Clarke, who issued his annual budget on Tuesday, the last before the general election which must take place by May 22, said there were no plans to make any "radical" changes.
"Moving to one system of taxation would be I think an extraordinary step," Clarke told Reuters as he left the conference hall.
"We've got the Inland Revenue and the Department of Social Security working much closer together than they used to in collecting those two taxes. But they work on very different principles."

Britain's 25 million taxpayers pay between 20p and 40p tax for every pound earned. At the same time up to 10 percent of their income is deducted from every wage packet to pay for national insurance - a separate tax that pays for the national health service and unemployment benefit.
Critics of the system claim Britain's finance ministers, past and present, have used the two-pronged system to give the illusion of lower taxes without actually reducing the overall tax burden.
On Tuesday, Clarke reduced the "standard" rate of tax to 23p in the pound from 24p last year, and down from the 33p rate when the Conservatives came to power in 1979.

But since 1979, the national insurance tax burden has been raised from a top rate of 6.5 percent of income to the current 10 percent, a near 54 percent increase. "It shows that if you delve beneath the numbers it is clear that the direct tax burden hasn't actually changed that much," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International. "In some cases, the tax take has actually picked up."
